questions.question:
What error, if any, does this raise and why?
```python
class Squad:
    def __init__(self, members):
        self.members = members
print(len(Squad([1, 2])))
```
questions.answer:
It raises TypeError: object of type 'Squad' has no len(). len() requires a __len__ method and will not guess the length from a stored list.

code:
class Squad:
    def __init__(self, members):
        self.members = members

print(len(Squad([1, 2])))  # TypeError

real example:
Calling len() on a wrapper that forgot to implement the length protocol fails loudly.

Predict the output:
```python
import abc
class NoiseMaker(metaclass=abc.ABCMeta):
    @abc.abstractmethod
    def make(self):
        ...
NoiseMaker.register(int)
print(issubclass(int, NoiseMaker))
```

questions.answer:

    @abc.abstractmethod
    def make(self): ...

NoiseMaker.register(int)

    def __len__(self): return len(self.items)
    def __getitem__(self, i): return self.items[i]

print(s[1])         # 20

Output: 3 2 1. iter(Down(3)) returns the object itself as its own iterator, and each next() decrements the stored n.

code:
class Down:
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n
    def __iter__(self): return self
    def __next__(self):
        if self.n == 0:
            raise StopIteration
        self.n -= 1
        return self.n + 1

it = iter(Down(3))
print(next(it), next(it), next(it))  # 3 2 1

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name, self.age = name, age
    def __repr__(self):
        return self.name
people = [Person('bob', 30), Person('alice', 25), Person('carol', 25)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p.age))
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (p.age, p.name)))
```
questions.answer:
Output: [alice, carol, bob] both times. sorted() extracts a key from each element via the lambda, so it never cares about the objects' types.

code:
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name, self.age = name, age
    def __repr__(self):
        return self.name

people = [Person('bob', 30), Person('alice', 25), Person('carol', 25)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p.age))
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (p.age, p.name)))

real example:
Sorting customer records by age or by name works on any object exposing those keys.

Output: [1, 2, 3]. Without a key, sort compares elements with __lt__ (plus the required comparisons) and prints them via __repr__.

code:
class Grade:
    def __init__(self, v): self.v = v
    def __lt__(self, other): return self.v < other.v
    def __repr__(self): return str(self.v)

print(sorted([Grade(3), Grade(1), Grade(2)]))  # [1, 2, 3]

real example:
Sorting events by time works once each event knows how to compare itself to another.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
class Base:
    pass
class Child(Base):
    pass
c = Child()
print(isinstance(c, Base))
print(isinstance(c, Child))
print(issubclass(Child, Base))
print(isinstance(Base, Child))
print(isinstance(c, (Base, str)))
```
questions.answer:
Output: True, True, True, False, True. isinstance checks subclasses and registered types; issubclass checks class inheritance; tuples mean OR over the types.

code:
class Base:
    pass

class Child(Base):
    pass

c = Child()
print(isinstance(c, Base))            # True
print(isinstance(c, Child))           # True
print(issubclass(Child, Base))        # True
print(isinstance(Base, Child))        # False
print(isinstance(c, (Base, str)))     # True

real example:
Tuple isinstance allows an API to accept any of several related types at once.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Left: def __add__(self, other): return 'left'. class Right: def __radd__(self, other): return 'right'. print(Left() + Right())
questions.answer:
Output: left. The left operand is always tried first; since Left.__add__ exists and returns 'left', Right.__radd__ is never reached.

code:
class Left:
    def __add__(self, other): return 'left'

class Right:
    def __radd__(self, other): return 'right'

print(Left() + Right())  # left

real example:
Forward methods take priority, so when both sides define the operation the left side wins.

questions.question: Predict the output. class Great: / def __init__(self): self.nums = [] / def __iadd__(self, other): self.nums.append(other); return self. x = Great(); y = x; x += 10; print(y.nums)
questions.answer:
Output: [10]. __iadd__ mutates the shared instance and returns self, so x and y alias the same object and both observe the appended value.

code:
class Great:
    def __init__(self): self.nums = []
    def __iadd__(self, other):
        self.nums.append(other)
        return self

x = Great()
y = x
x += 10
print(y.nums)  # [10]

real example:
In-place operators on mutable objects update all aliases pointing to that object.

questions.question: Find the bug. class Weird: / def __init__(self, v): self.v = v / def __iadd__(self, other): self.v += other  # note: no return. a = Weird(1); a += 1; print(a.v). Why does this crash?
questions.answer:
It crashes with AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'v'. += rebinds to whatever __iadd__ returns, and without a return statement that is None. Fix: return self.

code:
class Weird:
    def __init__(self, v): self.v = v
    def __iadd__(self, other):
        self.v += other
        return self

a = Weird(1)
a += 1
print(a.v)  # 2

real example:
In-place methods must return the instance; forgetting the return breaks every += use.

questions.answer:
Output: 4 7. With no __iadd__, q += 3 becomes q = q + 3, building a new Point(7); r still points to the original Point(4).

code:
class Point:

    def __add__(self, other):

q = Point(4)
r = q

questions.question: Predict the output. class Num: / def __init__(self, v): self.v = v / def __iadd__(self, o): return self.v + o. n = Num(3); n += 4; print(n, type(n).__name__)

questions.question: Predict the error. class F: / def __lt__(self, o): return True. What happens for 5 < F()?
questions.answer:
It raises TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'F'. int.__lt__ returns NotImplemented, and F defines no __gt__ to mirror <, so both sides fail.

code:
class F:
    def __lt__(self, o): return True

print(5 < F())  # TypeError
